messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 65
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Oceania
- Relationship Status: Widowed
- Occupation: Project Manager
- Trauma Type: Child's life-threatening illness
- Pcl5: 46

Thomas is a 65-year-old man of Oceania descent, a retired project manager who still consults part-time for a construction firm. He lives alone in the house he shared with his wife, who passed away three years ago. His children—a daughter and a son—both live in other cities, though he speaks with them by phone weekly. The trauma that reshaped his life began twelve years ago, when his daughter, then twenty-seven, was diagnosed with a rare and aggressive form of leukemia.

At the time, Thomas was managing a major hospital expansion project. He remembers sitting in his office, staring at blueprints, when his wife called with the news. In that moment, the colored lines on the paper blurred into meaningless streaks. He drove to the hospital, but the memory of that drive is a blank—a hole in his mind. Over the next eighteen months, he continued working, but he became preoccupied with schedules, checklists, risk mitigation plans. As a project manager, he had always believed that any problem could be broken down into tasks and solved. He applied that logic to his daughter’s illness: he researched treatment protocols, tracked her blood counts on a spreadsheet, and attended every appointment with a notebook. He felt a desperate need to control the uncontrollable.

His daughter went into remission, then relapsed. The second round of treatment was brutal. Thomas remembers the sound of the IV pumps, the way the antiseptic smell clung to his clothes. He began waking in the middle of the night, heart pounding, imagining he heard her crying out—even when she was at home, stable. He started avoiding the oncology wing when visiting her, taking the stairs instead of the elevator that passed the pediatric floor. The sight of other children with bald heads would bring a wave of nausea. He told himself he was just tired.

His daughter has been in full remission for eight years now. She is married, with two healthy children. Thomas should feel relief. Instead, he feels a constant low-level dread. The trauma never ended—it just changed shape. When his grandchildren get a cold, he becomes hypervigilant, checking their temperatures hourly, insisting they see a doctor for a runny nose. His daughter tells him he is overreacting. He knows she is right, but he cannot stop.

At work, he once prided himself on his calm under pressure. Now, any unexpected change in a project timeline triggers a surge of adrenaline. A subcontractor falling behind schedule sends his mind racing to worst-case scenarios—financial collapse, lawsuits, failure. He micromanages his team, rechecking every detail, which strains relationships. His colleagues say he seems “on edge,” and he has been passed over for a promotion because senior leadership feels he cannot handle the ambiguity of a larger role.

Socially, Thomas has withdrawn. He no longer attends community events or family gatherings unless absolutely necessary. The noise and unpredictability of large groups make his chest tighten. He feels safest alone in his home office, where he can control the environment—the lighting, the temperature, the background music. But even there, he is not at peace. He spent last night on the floor, unable to sleep, replaying the moment the doctor said the words “we need to talk about your daughter’s results.” He hears that phrase in his mind at least once a day.

He has started to avoid medical appointments himself. His annual physical is overdue, but the thought of sitting in a waiting room, hearing a pager go off, fills him with dread. He buys over-the-counter sleep aids and antacids to manage the chronic indigestion and insomnia. He told his daughter last week that he feels like he is still in that hospital room, only now there are no nurses, no doctors, no one to tell him what to do. He is the project manager of his own unrelenting fear.

Thomas does not think of himself as traumatized. He thinks of himself as a man who has been through a difficult time, and who is now perhaps “a bit wired.” He has not told anyone about the nightmares where his daughter’s face turns pale and the machines flatline. He has not mentioned that on some mornings, getting out of bed feels like moving through concrete. He just keeps adding tasks to his mental checklist, hoping that enough control will finally make the fear stop.
